The reading room reopens

After nineteen months behind hoarding, the first-floor reading room reopened to members on 12 March 2026 with 214 seats, a repaired roof lantern, and a quieter ventilation system than anyone expected.

The room has been in continuous use since the library opened in 1908, which is precisely why the refurbishment took as long as it did. Almost nothing in it could simply be replaced. The oak desks are original, and forty-one of them carry the shallow grooves worn by a century of elbows; the conservation team cleaned and rewaxed them rather than sanding them flat, on the argument that the wear is part of the record. The brass lamps were rewired in place. The plaster cornice, which had cracked in three places where the roof leaked, was cast from a mould taken off an undamaged section at the north end.

The leak was the reason for the closure. Water had been finding its way past the lantern glazing for at least a decade, and by the summer of 2024 it was running down the inside face of the north wall during heavy rain. Members reported buckets. The survey that followed found that the cast-iron glazing bars had corroded where the original putty had failed, and that the corrosion had lifted the bars enough to break the seal along most of the room's length. Replacing the putty alone would have bought perhaps two years. The decision, taken in October 2024, was to strip the lantern entirely, treat the ironwork, and reglaze with laminated glass matched to the original tint.

What changed, and what did not

The seat count is 214, up from 190, and the increase came entirely from reclaiming the two bays at the south end that had been walled off as a store in the 1970s. Members who remember the room from before will find the layout otherwise unchanged: the long desks still run east to west, the reference shelving still lines the north wall, and the enquiries desk is still immediately inside the double doors.

Ventilation is the change most people notice first, and it is the one the project team is quietest about, because it very nearly went wrong. The original scheme called for mechanical ventilation with ducts run above the new ceiling. It was abandoned after acoustic testing showed that the fan noise would sit at 42 decibels at desk level — audible, in a room where the ambient level is around 30. The scheme that replaced it reopened the Victorian passive stacks in the east and west walls, which had been blocked with rubble at some point before the war, and added small extract fans in the roof void that run only when carbon dioxide crosses a threshold. On most days they never run at all.

Power at the desks is new. Every seat now has a socket and a USB-C outlet, fitted into the desk edge in a housing that matches the oak. The library resisted this for years on the grounds that it would change the character of the room, and then conceded the obvious point that a reading room with no power is a reading room people leave at lunchtime.

Lighting is warmer than before — 2700 kelvin rather than the 4000 kelvin fittings installed in 2011 — and dimmable in four zones. The roof lantern does most of the work on a bright day, as it was designed to.

Using the digital archive

The digital archive moved during the closure and did not move back. It now occupies the second floor, in the room that was the map store, and it is open Tuesday to Saturday, from 10am to 5pm. There are four terminals. Booking is not required for a session under an hour, but is strongly advised on Saturdays, when the room is routinely full by eleven.

The archive holds 41,000 catalogued items: the borough's newspapers from 1841 onward, the photographic survey commissioned in 1936, the minute books of the library's own trustees, and — the collection that draws the most visitors — some 9,000 glass plate negatives from the Halloway studio, which operated on Hollow Lane from 1889 until it burned down in 1952. Roughly two thirds of the plates have been scanned. The rest are being worked through at a rate of about forty a week, which puts the end of the project some way into 2029.

Access is by member number. Anyone with a current membership can use the terminals; anyone without one can apply at the desk and start the same afternoon. Downloads are permitted for personal and academic use, and the archive staff will supply higher-resolution files on request, usually within a fortnight. Commercial use needs a licence, which is handled by the borough rather than the library.

The building fund

The refurbishment cost £2.4 million. Just over half came from the borough's capital programme, a third from a heritage grant, and the remainder — £310,000 — from members, in donations ranging from two pounds to sixty thousand. The board of trustees has asked that the donor board in the entrance hall list every contributor by name rather than by amount, which is why it is so long.

Attention now turns to the third floor, where the local studies collection has been sharing a room with the staff kitchen since 2018. No date has been set, and no money has been raised. The librarians are, by their own account, in no hurry to put up hoarding again.
